Which states have you crossed the economic nexus threshold in?

A private tracker for online and multi-channel sellers. Every state that levies a sales tax sets its own "economic nexus" threshold — a level of sales into that state past which the state can require you to register and collect its sales tax, no physical presence required. Enter your trailing-12-month sales into each state you sell into and get a per-state answer against that state's own published figure.

After using this, you can now see exactly which states you've crossed a registration threshold in and which you haven't, per state, against each one's own dollar and transaction-count rule — which used to mean cross-referencing fifty-one separate sets of figures by hand. See why the rule differs so much state to state, how this compares to an ongoing paid nexus-monitoring platform, or how this compares to tracking it in a spreadsheet yourself.

Selling on eBay, Etsy, Venmo, or a similar marketplace or payment app too? A crossed sales-tax threshold here is a separate question from whether a platform will send you a Form 1099-K — the 1099-K threshold checker answers that one.

Or import your orders (CSV)

Drop in an order export from Shopify, Etsy, Amazon or WooCommerce. The page finds the ship-to state, amount and date columns, keeps the last 12 months, totals each state, and estimates the date each uncrossed state would cross if your last 90 days of selling continued. The file is read in this browser and never uploaded.

StateSales, 12 moOrdersOf thresholdStatusProjected crossing

Projection is a straight-line estimate from your last 90 days, not a forecast, and it uses a trailing 12-month window; several states measure the prior or current calendar year instead. Amounts use the order subtotal where the file has one, so tax you collected is not counted as a sale. Refunds, rows with an unreadable state or date, and repeated order ids are skipped and counted above.

Add a state

Each state is checked on its own — sales in one state are never added to another's total, because that is not how the threshold works. Use a trailing-12-month figure; a few states measure differently — see the FAQ below.

Results

Sales figures and state selections stay on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Usage counts contain only feature names and are never sent anywhere.

Common questions

What is economic nexus for sales tax?

Since the Supreme Court's 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair decision, a state can require an out-of-state seller to collect and remit its sales tax once the seller's sales into that state cross a threshold the state sets for itself — no physical presence (office, warehouse, employee) required. Every state that levies a general sales tax has adopted its own version, each with its own dollar figure and, in some states, an added transaction-count test.

Do I add my sales from every state together to check the threshold?

No. Each state checks only the sales you made into that specific state, on its own. $80,000 into Idaho and $80,000 into Ohio does not combine into $160,000 for either state's own threshold — enter each state as its own row.

Do sales a marketplace already collected tax on still count toward my threshold?

In most states, yes — marketplace-facilitated sales (Amazon, Etsy, Walmart Marketplace collecting and remitting on your behalf) still count toward your own economic-nexus threshold in that state, even though the marketplace is the one currently remitting. Crossing the threshold can still create a registration or filing obligation for you once you sell outside that marketplace too. This tool counts every dollar you enter; it does not know which of your sales were marketplace-facilitated, so decide what to include based on your own state's marketplace-facilitator rule.

What happens if I cross a threshold and don't register?

States can generally assess back tax, penalties, and interest from the date nexus was established, not just from when you were caught — and in some states a responsible officer can be held personally liable for unremitted sales tax. This tool only estimates whether you've crossed a threshold; it does not calculate what you would owe or file anything on your behalf.

Why isn't this the same as a paid nexus-monitoring service like Avalara or TaxJar?

Those platforms connect directly to your sales channels, monitor your rolling totals continuously, calculate and file the actual returns, and charge an ongoing subscription for it. This tool is a free, one-time or periodic check you run by hand with numbers you already have — useful for a seller who wants to know where they stand today before an ongoing paid platform is worth the cost. See the full comparison.

Does every state use the same measurement period?

No. Most states look at the current or previous calendar year, but several (including Connecticut, Tennessee, Texas, and Vermont) use a trailing 12-month window instead, and a few states' own guidance differs in wording from state to state. This tool asks for a trailing-12-month figure as the safest common input, but does not model each state's exact measurement-period rule — confirm your specific state's counting window on its own department-of-revenue site.

No warranty. This tool is free and as-is. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and does not replace a qualified tax preparer or state guidance. Threshold figures are compiled from secondary sources (state department-of-revenue guidance as aggregated by third-party nexus-tracking publishers), not an independent fifty-state statute review — thresholds change by state legislation and this tool can be out of date. A "crossed" or "not crossed" result is a starting point for your own review, not a determination of a filing or registration obligation. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output, and for confirming any threshold with the state's own department of revenue, before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Free and open source. If it saved you from an unpleasant surprise, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-paid-nexus-monitoring-software.html.text:
← back to the tracker

This tracker vs. paid nexus-monitoring software

Avalara and TaxJar are the two names sellers hear most often for sales-tax nexus monitoring, and both are real, capable platforms doing a genuinely different job from this page. This free tracker answers one question -- which states have I crossed a threshold in, right now, with the numbers I already have -- without an account, an integration, or a subscription. Here is exactly where each tool fits.

What each one actually does

JobThis trackerAvalara / TaxJar (paid, ongoing)
How you check a thresholdType in your trailing-12-month sales by state, by hand, whenever you want to check.Connects to your sales channels via API and tallies your rolling totals automatically as orders come in.
How you find out you've crossed oneYou re-run the check yourself and read the result.Sends an automatic alert the moment a threshold is approached or crossed.
What happens after you've crossed a thresholdNothing -- it names the states, and you take it from there.Most plans can calculate and file the actual sales tax returns for you on an ongoing basis.
CostFree.Ongoing subscription, priced by transaction volume or number of states.
Where your sales data goesNowhere -- stays in your browser's local storage, never uploaded.Held on the platform's servers, which is what makes the continuous monitoring and filing possible.

Common questions

What does paid nexus-monitoring software like Avalara or TaxJar actually do that this tracker doesn't?

A paid platform connects directly to your sales channels (Shopify, Amazon, your payment processor) via API, continuously tallies your rolling sales by state as new orders come in, alerts you automatically the moment you approach or cross a threshold, and in most plans calculates and files the actual sales tax returns once you're registered. This tracker does none of the ongoing, connected, or filing parts -- it answers one question, once, with numbers you type in yourself.

When is a free one-time check enough, and when do I need an ongoing paid platform?

A one-time or periodic check is enough for a seller who wants to know where they stand today, especially one not yet close to any threshold or selling into only a handful of states. An ongoing paid platform earns its subscription once you're registered in multiple states and need returns actually calculated and filed on a recurring deadline, or once your sales are large and volatile enough that a threshold could be crossed between the times you'd remember to check by hand.

Does this tracker replace an accountant or a paid platform once I've crossed a threshold?

No. Crossing a threshold is the start of a registration and filing process, not the end of one -- you still need to register with the state, determine what's taxable, calculate the tax, and file on that state's schedule. This tracker's job stops at telling you which states to look into next.

Is my sales data safer in this tracker than in a paid platform?

This tracker never uploads anything -- every number you enter stays in your browser's local storage and is never sent to a server, so there's no account to breach and no data of yours held anywhere. A connected paid platform necessarily holds your sales data on its servers in order to do the continuous monitoring and filing it's built for; that's a reasonable tradeoff for the functionality, but it is a tradeoff this tracker doesn't ask you to make.

Their features are described from their own public marketing and documentation as of this writing and may have changed since.

vs-tracking-it-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← back to the tracker

This tracker vs. tracking thresholds in a spreadsheet

Every figure this tracker uses is public: each state's dollar threshold, its transaction-count test where one exists, and whether that test is combined with an AND or an OR. A spreadsheet can hold the same 51 rows. Transcribing them correctly, keeping the AND/OR logic right for the states that pair the two tests, and noticing when a state changes its rule is the part that gets skipped when you need an answer today.

What each approach actually does

JobA spreadsheet you buildThis tracker
Where the 51 jurisdictions' figures come fromYou look each one up and type it in, then keep it current yourself.Already built in, compiled from named, dated sources.
Handling the ~16 states with a transaction-count testYou have to notice which states pair it with AND vs. OR and write two different formulas.Applies the right rule per state automatically.
A state that requires both figures together but you've only entered salesA formula that isn't written to catch this will silently return crossed or not-crossed either way.Says outright it needs a transaction count before it will guess.
A state with no sales tax at allYou have to remember to exclude Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon or a large number there reads as crossed.Already knows those five states have no threshold to cross.
CostFree, but your time to build and keep it correct.Free.
Where your sales data goesWherever you save the file.Nowhere — stays in your browser's local storage, never uploaded.

Common questions

Can I just build a spreadsheet to track this instead?

Yes. Every figure this tracker uses — each state's dollar threshold, its transaction-count test where one exists, and whether that test is combined with an AND or an OR — is public information you can type into a spreadsheet yourself. Building it means transcribing all 51 jurisdictions correctly, including the roughly sixteen that pair a transaction count onto the dollar figure, and updating any cell a state changes (Illinois dropped its 200-transaction alternative entirely as of 2026-01-01).

What does a spreadsheet not do that this tracker does?

Keep the AND/OR logic right without you re-deriving it per state. Connecticut and New York require both the dollar figure and a transaction count together (AND) — most other transaction-count states need only one or the other (OR). A spreadsheet formula that treats every state the same way will misjudge Connecticut or New York specifically. This tracker also states outright when it needs a transaction count it doesn't have, rather than defaulting to a silent guess, and it already knows which states levy no sales tax at all so a large number there never reads as crossed.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, if you want to do more with the numbers than check a threshold — combine nexus tracking with other tax reporting, chart your trailing sales over time, or keep a running history from filing period to filing period. This tracker holds only what you've entered right now; a spreadsheet you build and save yourself can be extended to do anything you can formula your way into.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the tracker runs entirely in your browser. Whatever you enter is saved to this browser's local storage between visits and never sent to a server, the same as a spreadsheet file that never leaves your own computer.

This page names no specific product — it compares against the generic method of tracking economic-nexus thresholds in a spreadsheet, not a competing tool.

why-does-economic-nexus-differ-by-state..text:
← Economic Nexus Threshold Tracker

Why does economic nexus differ by state?

Sales tax is a state and local tax, not a federal one, so when the Supreme Court's 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair decision let states tax out-of-state sellers based on sales volume instead of physical presence, it did not hand down one national number. Each state legislature wrote its own version. Here is why the figures land where they do and why they keep changing one state at a time.

Open the free economic nexus threshold tracker

Where the common $100,000 figure came from

South Dakota's own law -- $100,000 in sales or 200 transactions in the current or prior calendar year -- was the specific test the Supreme Court had in front of it and found constitutionally reasonable. Most states that adopted economic nexus in the year or two after the ruling copied that figure directly rather than defend a different number of their own in court, which is why $100,000 is still the most common threshold today.

Why a few states set a higher figure

California, New York, and Texas each set $500,000 instead. All three already had large sales tax bases from physical-presence sellers before Wayfair, so a higher bar mainly excludes smaller out-of-state sellers rather than giving up meaningful revenue from the sellers a lower figure would have added. Alabama and Mississippi sit in between at $250,000.

Why the 200-transaction test is disappearing

A pure transaction count can catch a seller with trivial revenue -- 200 transactions at $10 each is $2,000 in total sales, far below any state's dollar threshold, but enough to trigger a registration obligation under a strict either/or reading. States noticed this was capturing small sellers they never intended to reach, and have been dropping the transaction-count leg one at a time since 2019: Colorado, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Wisconsin, South Dakota itself, and most recently Illinois (effective 2026-01-01) now use revenue alone. Roughly a third of states still keep some form of the test, so this is an active, ongoing shift rather than a settled rule -- check the current figure for any state you're close to a threshold in.

AND versus OR: the one distinction worth knowing

In every state that still pairs a revenue figure with a transaction count, crossing either one alone is normally enough (an "OR" test) -- except Connecticut and New York, which currently require both together ("AND"). A seller who clears New York's $500,000 revenue figure but has fewer than 100 transactions has not crossed New York's threshold; a seller who clears both has.

States with no threshold at all

Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon levy no general statewide sales tax, so there is no economic-nexus threshold to cross there regardless of sales volume.

Common questions

Why isn't there one national economic nexus threshold?

Sales tax is a state and local tax in the United States, not a federal one, and South Dakota v. Wayfair (2018) upheld each state's own power to define when an out-of-state seller owes it -- the Supreme Court set the constitutional floor (a state's rule has to be reasonable, and South Dakota's $100,000-or-200-transactions test was found to be), not a single number every state must use. Congress has not passed a federal standard, so each state legislature sets its own.

Why did South Dakota's original $100,000 or 200 transactions become the most common figure?

Because it was the specific test the Supreme Court had in front of it and upheld, most states that adopted economic nexus in 2018-2019 copied it directly rather than defending a new figure of their own in court. States that already had large physical-presence sales tax bases before Wayfair (California, New York, Texas) had less incentive to copy South Dakota's number and set their own higher figures instead.

Why are states removing the 200-transaction test?

The transaction-count test was flagged early as capturing small, low-dollar sellers a state never intended to reach -- 200 transactions at $10 each is $2,000 in sales, far below any state's revenue threshold, yet it still creates a registration obligation under a strict OR reading. Colorado, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Wisconsin, South Dakota itself, Illinois, and others have dropped the transaction-count leg since 2019, leaving revenue as the only test -- a trend states keep following one at a time rather than all at once, which is exactly why this remains a state-by-state question rather than a settled one.

What is the difference between an AND state and an OR state?

In an OR state (most of the ones that still keep a transaction test), meeting either the revenue figure or the transaction count is enough on its own to cross the threshold. In an AND state -- currently Connecticut and New York -- a seller has to meet both the revenue figure and the transaction count together; meeting only one, however far over it, does not cross the threshold by itself.

Does a state with no sales tax have an economic nexus rule?

No. Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon levy no general statewide sales tax, so there is nothing for an economic-nexus threshold to trigger. (Alaska has local sales taxes in some municipalities, administered separately from any statewide economic-nexus program.)

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, or financial advice. State thresholds change by legislation; verify the current figure with the specific state's department of revenue before relying on any number here.
